Parallel Processing

Source: vignettes/parallel-processing.Rmd
parallel-processing.Rmd

Local Machine

When parallel_processing within forecast_time_series() is set to “local_machine”, each time series (including training models on the entire data set) is ran in parallel on the users local machine. Each time series will run on a separate core of the machine. Hyperparameter tuning, model refitting, and model averaging will be ran sequentially, which cannot be done in parallel since a parallel process is already running on the machine for each time series. This works well for data that contains many time series where you might only want to run a few simpler models, and in scenarios where cloud computing is not available.

If parallel_processing is set to NULL and inner_parallel is set to TRUE within forecast_time_series, then each time series is ran sequentially but the hyperparameter tuning and model refitting are ran in parallel. This works great for data that has a limited number of time series where you want to run a lot of back testing and build dozens of models within Finn.

With inner_parallel set to TRUE, Finn starts one pool of worker processes, reuses it across time series and modeling steps, and lets the tune package use it by temporarily registering it as the future plan. Finn restores your own future plan when the run finishes. The pool has at most num_cores workers (by default every available core but one, respecting container CPU limits), and never more than a modeling step can use: the hyperparameter combinations times the validation splits, or the number of back-test splits. Each worker needs roughly 400 MB of memory before any data is loaded, so leave enough memory headroom when choosing num_cores.

Parallel AI Agent Workflows

set_agent_info() accepts one ellmer Chat or chat_copilot() object as an immutable configuration template. Every iterate_forecast() time-series combo receives an independent, empty-history session from that template, whether combos run sequentially or in parallel. For parallel execution, Finn sends the template through the standard foreach serialization path and creates each session inside the series workflow after it reaches the worker. A session persists across iterations for its own series but is never shared with another series.

Ellmer-backed parallel runs require ellmer 0.4.0 or later in the main process and every worker R library. The public Chat$clone(deep = TRUE) method preserves the provider, model, parameters, tools, and credentials without rebuilding Chat objects through internal ellmer APIs. With Azure OpenAI API-key authentication, the default ellmer 0.4 credential callback is serialized with the template, so worker task payloads must be treated as sensitive. A custom credentials callback that reads an environment variable or obtains a token at request time requires that credential source to be available from every worker process.

Copilot-backed workflows recreate configuration rather than cloning an ellmer Chat. Each worker needs GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.93 or later, processx 3.9.0 or later, and available environment-token or GitHub CLI authentication. CLI version and option checks are cached in memory per process and executable; each worker checks independently, and executable changes trigger revalidation. Credentials are resolved on the worker and never serialized in the template. Copilot starts a tool-disabled process per request, replays that series’ history through stdin, and saves CLI-local state under the worker’s R temporary directory. Consider request quotas and CLI startup costs when choosing concurrency; a driver-local executable path or login is not automatically available on a Spark cluster. See the AI Agent vignette for setup and data handling requirements.

Within Azure using Spark

To leverage the full power of Finn, running within Azure is the best choice in building production ready forecasts that can easily scale. The most efficient way to run Finn is to set parallel_processing to “spark” within forecast_time_series(). This will run each time series in parallel across a spark compute cluster.

Sparklyr is a great R package that allows you to run R code across a spark cluster. A user simply has to connect to a spark cluster then run Finn. Below is an example on how you can run Finn using spark on Azure Databricks. Also check out the growing R support with using spark on Azure Synapse.

# load CRAN libraries
library(finnts)
library(sparklyr)

# connect to spark cluster
options(sparklyr.log.console = TRUE)

sc <- sparklyr::spark_connect(method = "databricks")

# call Finn with spark parallel processing
hist_data <- timetk::m4_monthly %>%
  dplyr::rename(Date = date) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(id = as.character(id))

data_sdf <- sparklyr::copy_to(sc, hist_data, "data_sdf", overwrite = TRUE)

run_info <- set_run_info(
  project_name = "finn_fcst",
  run_name = "spark_run_1",
  path = "/dbfs/mnt/example/folder" # important that you mount an ADLS path
)

forecast_time_series(
  run_info = run_info,
  input_data = data_sdf,
  combo_variables = c("id"),
  target_variable = "value",
  date_type = "month",
  forecast_horizon = 3,
  parallel_processing = "spark",
  return_data = FALSE
)

# return the outputs as a spark data frame
finn_output_tbl <- get_forecast_data(
  run_info = run_info,
  return_type = "sdf"
)

The above example runs each time series on a separate core on a spark cluster. On an Azure Synapse Spark pool, connect to the pool’s Spark installation instead, and give set_run_info() a path under your ADLS mount, which starts with /synfs:

sc <- sparklyr::spark_connect(
  master = "yarn",
  version = "3.5",
  spark_home = "/opt/spark",
  config = sparklyr::spark_config()
)

Mount ADLS with fileCacheTimeout = 0. The default mount caches file listings and contents for 120 seconds, so outputs that one node just wrote can look missing or out of date on another. Finn waits and reads such outputs again, but a mount without the cache avoids that wait; in our Synapse tests it didn’t slow runs down.

mssparkutils.fs.mount(
  "abfss://<container>@<storage account>.dfs.core.windows.net",
  "/finn",
  list(linkedService = "<linked service>", fileCacheTimeout = 0)
)

run_info <- set_run_info(
  project_name = "finn_fcst",
  run_name = "spark_run_1",
  path = mssparkutils.fs.getMountPath("/finn")
)

Finn reconnects to Spark at the start of each Spark step, reusing the connection’s method and configuration. By default sparklyr then copies the driver’s R packages to the executors again before the step’s first task. When every executor already has the same R package library as the driver, such as a Synapse Spark pool or a Databricks cluster with the packages installed on the pool or cluster, you can skip that copy by adding config$sparklyr.apply.packages <- FALSE to the connection config. Keep the default when executors may be missing packages, because their tasks would fail when loading Finn.

Spark 3.5 works with sparklyr 1.8.6, the version installed on Synapse Spark 3.5 pools. Spark 4 needs sparklyr 1.9.1 or later.

You can also submit multiple time series where each time series runs on a separate spark executor (VM) and then leverage the cores on that executor to run things like hyperparameter tuning or model refitting in parallel. This creates two levels of parallelization. One at the time series level, then another when doing things like hyperparameter tuning within a specific time series. To do that set inner_parallel to TRUE in forecast_time_series().

Spark runs spark.executor.cores time series at once on each executor (divided by spark.task.cpus when that is set). It doesn’t limit the cores an R process can use, so when num_cores is NULL, Finn gives each time series an equal share of the executor node’s cores, minus one for the series itself. On 32-core nodes, spark.executor.cores set to 1 gives each series about 31 inner workers, and 2 gives two series about 15 workers each. Use 1 for heavy work within each series, such as large hyperparameter grids, many back tests or feature selection, and 2 or more to run more series at once. If spark.executor.cores isn’t set (Databricks runs one series per core by default), there are no spare cores and each series uses a single inner worker. Set it with the “spark.executor.cores” argument when configuring your spark connection, using sparklyr or the cluster manager within the Azure resource. This sizing assumes one executor per node and a driver with the same node size as the executors; otherwise set num_cores in forecast_time_series() to the number of inner workers each series should use.

Inner workers run outside the Spark JVM, so they share only the node memory Spark doesn’t reserve. For example, with spark.executor.memory = "220g" on a 252 GB node, about 30 GB remains for all inner workers on that node.

forecast_time_series() will be looking for a variable called “sc” to use when submitting tasks to the spark cluster, so make sure you use that as the variable name when connecting to spark. Also it’s important that you mount your spark session to an Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) account, and provide the mounted path to where you’d like your Finn results to be written to within set_run_info().

Spark executors run Finn with their own R package library. Before installing a new version of Finn on a cluster, upgrade that library to the minimum package versions listed in Finn’s DESCRIPTION file, including tune 2.0.1 or later.
